blocks.text: *Damage types, elements, and matchups. Unwritten uses a pre-Renewal Ragnarok-style combat model.*
The three damage types
Every hit is one of three types, and each behaves differently:

items: **Physical** — uses your **Attack** against the target's **Defense**. Can miss, can crit.
**Magic** — uses your **Magic Attack** against **Magic Defense**. **Never misses**, and **cannot crit** — except in a **Sniper**'s hands, where it crits like a physical hit and ignores Magic Defense.
**Critical** — a forced critical hit that **ignores Defense**.

blocks.text: Three always-on rules
These are hard rules the combat math always honors:

items: **Critical hits ignore Defense** — armor doesn't save you from a crit.
**Magic never misses** — accuracy and dodge don't apply to spells.
**Tanks resist mages** — high Defense and HP hold up well against the magic arc, so a durable build is the natural answer to casters.

blocks.text: The archetype triangle *(design intent)*
Builds are meant to settle into a rock-paper-scissors of three archetypes:

items: **AGI / LUK (crit)** beats **STR / VIT (tank)** — crit partly bypasses Defense.
**STR / VIT (tank)** beats **INT / DEX (mage)** — HP and Magic Defense soak the burst.
**INT / DEX (mage)** beats **AGI / LUK (crit)** — magic ignores dodge.

text: These are intended tendencies (not absolute counters), and the exact numbers are still being tuned.

blocks.text: Elements

Every monster has an **element**, and it works both ways: its ordinary attacks land as that element, and it is hit as that element. Element against element changes the damage — the classic Ragnarok matchup web. You are **Neutral** until a converter says otherwise. The elements are:
**Neutral · Water · Earth · Fire · Wind · Poison · Holy · Dark · Ghost · Undead**

For example, Fire is strong into Earth, Water is strong into Fire, and Holy bites hardest into Undead and Dark. A skill keeps its own element — a fire bolt is Fire whoever casts it; only ordinary attacks take the attacker's element.

A monster's element has a **level, 1 to 4**. The higher the level, the more it shrugs off what it resists and the harder it falls to what it is weak to. At **level 3 and 4** a monster can **heal** from the element it resists most — hit a level-4 Fire creature with Fire and it regains health instead of losing it.

**Converters** change your element for **5:00**. An *Elemental Converter* makes your ordinary attacks land as its element; an *Armor Converter* makes you hit as its element, at level 1. A new converter replaces the old one of the same kind, and one of each can run together. There are four of each — **Flame** (Fire), **Frost** (Water), **Seismic** (Earth) and **Lightning** (Wind) — and each drops from monsters of its own element.
Monster sizes *(planned matchup)*

Monsters come in **Small, Medium and Large** sizes (see *Monsters*), and weapon types are intended to matter against size — a dagger shines against small swarms, while heavy two-handers are built to bite into large foes. *(This size-vs-weapon matchup is designed but not yet switched on in combat.)*
Status ailments
Skills can inflict lasting conditions:

items: **Damage over time:** Burn, Poison, Bleed
**Control:** Stun, Freeze, Silence

blocks.text: Those six are the whole list. **Weakening isn't an ailment** — being slowed, blinded, or made to take extra damage is the same thing as any buff, just pointed the other way: one number on your sheet moved down for a while. Move speed, accuracy and damage taken are ordinary stats, so a skill lowers them exactly the way another skill raises them.
Buffs, debuffs & stacks

Anything lasting that sits on you or an enemy is a **state** — buffs and debuffs work the same way underneath. Your own states show as icons on the right edge of the screen, counting down; a monster's or another player's show on the panel at the top of the screen when you click them.

Some states **stack**. Each stack carries its own strength and its own timer, and the total is simply the sum — ten stacks of +3% attack is +30% attack. When a stack expires, only that one drops; the rest keep running. An icon shows its count when it's holding more than one.

**Death clears everything.** Nothing timed survives dying — no buff, no debuff, no banked damage, no charges. That holds for you and for monsters alike, so nothing comes back still carrying what killed it. Logging out or travelling does **not** clear them: they wait, paused, and carry on with the time they had left when you come back.
Taunt
A taunted enemy is doing three things at once, for as long as it lasts:

items: **Locked onto whoever taunted it** — a ranged enemy loses its standoff and closes in instead of kiting.
**It cannot use skills.** Only its ordinary swings.
**No pause between swings.** Its swing *rate* is untouched — the taunt removes the gaps, it doesn't make it faster.

blocks.text: Its **passives still fire**. A taunt takes away choices, and a passive isn't one. These rules belong to the taunt itself, so they hold for whatever it lands on.
Charges

A few skills hand you a burst of **charges** at once — several stacks sharing one window, spent one at a time. Casting a skill might grant 5 charges, and each qualifying hit spends one until they're gone or the window closes.

**A charge is spent on use, and never refunded.** Whatever happens afterwards — the swing was cancelled, the dash hit a wall, the target died mid-cast — the charge is gone. That's deliberate: if cancelling gave charges back, cancel-spam would be free.
The four kinds of charge you'll meet:

items: **Parry charges** — each one erases a whole incoming hit. No damage, no defense math, then the charge is gone.
**Brace charges** — each one holds a hit back instead of erasing it. The damage is banked, and the whole bill lands at once when the window ends.

**Attack charges** — each one makes a single outgoing attack land harder, and is spent **whether it hits or misses** (the charge paid for making the attack, not for landing it). The bonus applies *before* the target's armor, so it's worth more against tanky foes. There's a mirror version that makes an attack land softer.
**Skill charges** — a count a skill spends as it runs, like each strike of a long combo.

blocks.text: Some charge piles are sized by **how fast you swing** rather than by a fixed number, so a faster character genuinely gets more of them.
Combo skills

Some skills **require** a state before they'll do anything. If you don't have it, the skill simply doesn't fire — no animation, no cooldown, no mana spent. Skills that cash in a state always calculate their power from what you're carrying **before** spending it, so a finisher gets full value from every stack it consumes.
A skill that triggers off your hits can never chain into itself, so a combo can't spiral out of control — its charges are its budget, and that's the ceiling.
Weapon out or put away

Your weapon is either **in your hands** or **put away on your body**. Press **X** to take it out or put it away. Attacking, or pressing one of your weapon's skills, takes it out first, and the attack or skill follows the moment it is in hand. Starting to walk (**Shift**) or to sprint (**V**) puts it away: you can only sprint with your weapon put away.

Taking it out or putting it away takes **0.2 seconds plus 0.006 seconds for each point of the weapon's weight** — 0.74 seconds for a weapon of weight 90, about 1 second for the Greatsword at weight 133. Your legs keep moving while your arms do it.
With your weapon put away, and **5 seconds** gone by since you last dealt or took a blow:

items: your health and mana come back **twice as fast** on their own — healing skills and potions heal what they always heal
monsters notice you from **half** the distance they otherwise would

blocks.text: Monsters live by the same rules: they take their weapons out while they hunt and put them away when they give up.
